opus-5.5.text:
Yes, I think that's one of the really striking contrasts. If you show a young child a picture book with a cartoon giraffe, a few simple lines, a yellow shape with brown blotches, they can then go to the zoo and point at the real animal and say "giraffe!" Sometimes they've only seen one or two drawings. The drawing is wildly different from the real thing at the pixel level: different colours, no texture, no three-dimensionality, often exaggerated proportions. Yet the child makes the leap almost effortlessly.

Compare that with how deep learning systems have typically learned. Classic image classifiers needed thousands or millions of labelled examples, and even then they were brittle in odd ways. Train on photographs and test on sketches, and performance would often collapse. The child seems to extract something like the *concept*, the abstract structure of what makes a giraffe a giraffe, whereas the networks were picking up much more on surface statistics like textures.

That said, I want to be careful about how much to read into it. A child isn't starting from scratch. They have hundreds of millions of years of evolution building priors into the visual system, and by the time they're looking at picture books they've had a couple of years of continuous, rich, embodied visual experience. So the fair comparison isn't "one drawing versus a million images." It's more like a heavily pre-trained system doing few-shot learning. Interestingly, that's roughly what we now see with large pre-trained models: after enormous amounts of pre-training, they can often recognise something from a sketch, or learn a new category from a handful of examples. So part of the gap has closed, but the cost has moved into the pre-training.

Even granting all that, I think humans are still far more sample efficient overall. A child learns language from perhaps tens of millions of words. Frontier language models are trained on trillions. That's a gap of something like five orders of magnitude. It suggests that there are big algorithmic insights we haven't yet found, or that biology is using inductive biases we don't understand well.

That matters a lot for thinking about AI's trajectory. One view is that the inefficiency is fine: we can just pay for it with compute and data, and scaling will keep working. But if we start running out of high-quality data, sample efficiency becomes the bottleneck, and whoever closes the gap could see a large and possibly quite sudden jump in capabilities. The existence proof of the human child tells us that much greater efficiency is *possible*. We just don't know how close we are to finding it. For someone thinking about risk, that's uncomfortable, because it means progress could come not just from the steady, observable growth of compute but from a conceptual breakthrough that's much harder to forecast.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find genuinely puzzling, and I think it's one of the more interesting open questions about how current systems relate to human intelligence. The standard observation is that children can see a few line drawings of a giraffe — maybe a single cartoon in a picture book — and then go to the zoo and recognise a real giraffe, which is a totally different kind of visual input. The drawing is two-dimensional, it's a handful of black lines, it has none of the texture or colour or depth of the real thing. And yet the child makes the connection immediately. Whereas the classic story about deep learning is that these systems need thousands or millions of labelled examples to learn a category, and even then they can be quite brittle about distribution shift — you train on photographs and the model struggles with sketches, or vice versa.

So on the face of it, that looks like a huge gap in sample efficiency, and people sometimes use it as evidence that deep learning is doing something fundamentally different from, and inferior to, what brains do.

But I think there are a couple of things to be careful about here. The first is that the comparison isn't really like for like. The child isn't learning from one drawing. By the time a child is two or three, they've had years of continuous high-bandwidth visual experience — their eyes have been taking in something like a video stream every waking moment. They've learned an enormous amount about edges, shapes, how objects behave in three dimensions, what counts as a boundary. So the one drawing is a tiny bit of additional data on top of a vast prior. And then of course there's evolution, which has spent hundreds of millions of years shaping the visual system so that it's well suited to picking out objects. When you count all of that, the human isn't nearly as sample efficient as the "one drawing" framing suggests.

And interestingly, the deep learning story has been moving in that direction too. The modern approach isn't to train a classifier from scratch on labelled giraffes. It's to pretrain a very large model on an enormous amount of unlabelled data, and then the system can often recognise a new category from just a few examples, or even from a text description. That's a lot closer to what the child is doing — a huge amount of general learning, and then very rapid adaptation. So the gap in what you might call "few-shot" efficiency has narrowed a lot, though I don't think it's closed.

The second thing I'd say is that there does still seem to be something to the drawing case specifically, which is about abstraction. The child seems to be extracting the structural essence — long neck, four legs, spots — and treating the drawing and the animal as instances of the same abstract thing. There's an argument that human perception is organised around this kind of compositional, structured representation in a way that pure pattern-matching systems aren't, and that this is why we generalise so robustly. I'm genuinely uncertain how much of that is true. Some of the recent models do seem to get some of this, but it's often hard to tell whether they've learned the abstraction or just seen enough sketches in their training set.

Why I think this matters for the bigger questions I care about is that it bears on how we should forecast progress. If the sample efficiency gap reflects a deep architectural difference, then scaling current methods might hit a wall, and you'd need genuinely new ideas before you get to systems with human-like general capability. If instead it's mostly about the amount and kind of pretraining data, then it's more a question of resources, and the trajectory looks a lot steeper. My own view is that it's probably somewhere in the middle — there's likely some missing ingredient around structured, data-efficient learning, but I've been repeatedly surprised by how much of what looked like a fundamental limitation turned out to be addressable with scale and better training. So I try not to lean too heavily on the "children are so much more efficient" intuition as a reason for complacency about timelines.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a really interesting comparison. A child can see a drawing of a giraffe in a picture book, and then, when they see an actual giraffe, recognise it—even though the drawing may look quite different from the real thing. That suggests they’ve learned something more abstract than just the particular visual features of the example.

But we have to be careful about what we’re counting as a sample. The child has already had an enormous amount of visual experience, and they’ve learned something about pictures: that these marks on a page represent things in the world. So it isn’t learning from one example starting from nothing. It’s bringing a lot of prior learning to bear.

The interesting question, then, is how efficiently a system can use that background experience to learn a new concept, and how well that concept transfers to a different setting. The child’s ability is striking, but the comparison alone doesn’t tell us whether deep learning can achieve the same thing, or what would be needed to get there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a fascinating comparison, but it’s quite hard to know what the right accounting is. A child can see a drawing of an elephant and then recognise a real elephant, which looks like an extraordinary feat of generalisation. The drawing leaves out most of the information in the real scene, yet somehow the child picks up on the relevant structure.

But the child isn’t starting from scratch. They’ve already had a great deal of visual experience, and they have the benefit of structures that evolved over a very long time. So comparing the number of elephant pictures a child has seen with the number a neural network needs may miss a lot of what made that learning possible.

That doesn’t make the achievement any less interesting. It suggests that humans have very useful ways of representing the world, which let us transfer what we learn between quite different settings. The question is how much of that comes from prior learning, how much is built in, and whether artificial systems can acquire something similar. I’d be cautious about drawing a firm conclusion about the limits of deep learning from the comparison alone.
